instruction: What is an upper/lower split and who is it best for?
output: An upper/lower split divides training into upper body days (chest, back, shoulders, arms) and lower body days (quads, hamstrings, glutes, calves). It is best for intermediate lifters who can train 4 days per week, allowing each muscle group to be hit twice weekly with adequate recovery. A typical schedule is upper Monday, lower Tuesday, rest Wednesday, upper Thursday, lower Friday, then rest Saturday and Sunday. This split offers more volume per muscle group than full-body but more frequency than a bro split, making it efficient for strength and muscle growth.

instruction: How do I structure a 4-day upper/lower split for muscle growth?
output: Upper day A: horizontal push (bench press, 3x8-12), horizontal pull (bent-over row, 3x8-12), overhead press (3x8-12), biceps curls (3x10-15), triceps extensions (3x10-15). Lower day A: squat variation (3x6-10), Romanian deadlift (3x8-12), leg press (3x10-15), calf raises (4x12-20). Upper day B: incline press (3x8-12), lat pulldown (3x8-12), lateral raises (3x12-15), face pulls (3x15-20), hammer curls (3x10-15). Lower day B: deadlift variation (3x5-8), front squat or leg press (3x8-12), leg curls (3x10-15), calf raises (4x12-20). Rest 2 to 3 minutes between compounds, 60 to 90 seconds for isolations.

instruction: What is a push/pull/legs (PPL) split and how many days per week should I run it?
output: PPL splits training into push days (chest, shoulders, triceps), pull days (back, biceps, rear delts), and leg days (quads, hamstrings, glutes, calves). Most people run it 6 days per week as PPL PPL rest, hitting each muscle group twice weekly. It is ideal for intermediate to advanced lifters who can handle higher frequency and have 60 to 90 minutes per session. A 3-day per week PPL (e.g., push Monday, pull Wednesday, legs Friday) works for beginners but provides half the weekly volume, so progression is slower.

instruction: Can I do push/pull/legs as a 3-day per week routine?
output: Yes, a 3-day PPL works for beginners or those with limited time, but each muscle group is trained only once per week. This lower frequency means you need higher volume per session: 12 to 16 working sets per muscle group per week, all done in one day. For example, push day would include 4 chest exercises, 3 shoulder exercises, and 3 triceps exercises, which can lead to 90 minute sessions. Most people see better results with a 3-day full-body or 4-day upper/lower than a 3-day PPL, as twice weekly frequency is superior for growth.

instruction: What are the pros and cons of full-body training 3 times per week?
output: Pros: trains each muscle group 3 times weekly, excellent for beginners to learn compound movements, time-efficient (45 to 60 minute sessions), and allows more recovery between sessions. Cons: lower per-muscle volume per session (only 2 to 3 exercises per muscle group), can be systemically fatiguing as legs are hit every session, and advanced lifters may need more volume than full-body allows. Full-body works best for the first 6 to 12 months of training or for those who can only train 2 to 3 days per week. After that, most switch to upper/lower or PPL.

instruction: How do I choose between upper/lower and push/pull/legs?
output: Choose upper/lower if you can train 4 days per week and want shorter sessions (45 to 60 minutes) with twice weekly frequency for all muscles. Choose PPL if you can train 6 days per week, enjoy longer sessions (60 to 90 minutes), and want to specialize in certain lifts or bring up lagging body parts. Upper/lower is better for strength-focused lifters because compounds are less fatigued than on PPL where legs have their own day. For most intermediate lifters with 4 to 5 days available, upper/lower offers the best balance of frequency, volume, and recovery.

instruction: What exercises should I never skip on a full-body day?
output: At least one squat pattern (goblet squat, barbell squat, or leg press), one hinge pattern (Romanian deadlift or hip thrust), one horizontal push (bench press or push-up), one horizontal pull (row variation), and one overhead press. These five movements cover all major muscle groups and movement patterns. If time is limited, prioritize the squat and hinge as they work the largest muscle mass and most joints. Add one vertical pull (pull-up or lat pulldown) and one core exercise (plank or leg raise) when possible.

instruction: How many exercises per muscle group should I do on an upper day?
output: On an upper day, do 2 to 3 chest exercises, 2 to 3 back exercises, 1 to 2 shoulder exercises, and 1 to 2 biceps and triceps exercises each. For example: 2 chest (bench press + incline dumbbell), 2 back (pull-ups + seated row), 1 shoulder (lateral raises), 1 bicep (curls), 1 tricep (pushdowns). Total 7 to 9 exercises per upper session, with 3 to 4 sets each. Keep volume moderate (12 to 18 total sets per upper day) to avoid exceeding 20 sets per muscle group weekly, which leads to junk volume.

instruction: Can I add arm isolations every day on PPL?
output: You can add arm work on both push and pull days, but limit frequency to avoid overuse injuries. On push day, triceps get worked indirectly from pressing; add 2 to 3 sets of triceps isolations (pushdowns or skullcrushers) at the end. On pull day, biceps get indirect work from rows and pull-ups; add 2 to 3 sets of curls. Do not add extra arm isolations on leg day unless you have extra time and recovery capacity. Training arms 4 times per week (2 push + 2 pull) is sufficient for growth; more than 6 direct arm sessions weekly leads to tendonitis for most people.

instruction: How do I progress on a full-body routine week to week?
output: Use double progression: stay in a rep range like 6 to 10 for compounds. When you hit 10 reps on all sets, increase weight by 5 to 10 pounds and drop back to 6 reps. For isolations, use an 8 to 12 rep range with the same logic. Add 1 set per exercise every 2 to 3 weeks until you reach 4 to 5 sets, then deload. Track your top set weights each session; as a beginner, aim to add 2.5 to 5 pounds to squat, bench, and row every 1 to 2 weeks. After 12 to 16 weeks of linear progression, switch to periodized programming like 5/3/1 or upper/lower.

instruction: Should I deadlift on lower body day or back day?
output: Conventional deadlifts are primarily a posterior chain exercise (hamstrings, glutes, lower back), so they fit best on lower body day. On an upper/lower split, deadlift on lower day before squats or on a separate dedicated deadlift day. On PPL, deadlifts are often placed on pull day because they involve the back heavily, but this can fatigue your lower back before rows. A better approach: alternate deadlifts with squats every lower day, or do deadlifts first on pull day followed by vertical pulls, keeping horizontal rows for the end. For most intermediates, deadlifting once per week with 3 to 5 working sets is sufficient.

instruction: How many sets per week for each muscle group on upper/lower vs PPL?
output: On upper/lower (4 days), aim for 12 to 18 sets weekly per major muscle group: chest (12-16), back (14-18), quads (12-16), hamstrings (10-14), shoulders (10-14). On PPL (6 days), aim for 15 to 22 sets weekly due to higher frequency, but avoid exceeding 25 sets per muscle group. For example, chest gets 8 sets on push day A and 8 on push day B = 16 weekly. Smaller muscles like biceps and triceps need only 8 to 12 sets weekly regardless of split. Beginners start at the lower end (10-12 sets), intermediates at the middle (14-18), advanced at the higher end (18-22).

instruction: Can I do cardio on the same day as upper/lower or PPL training?
output: Yes, do cardio after lifting or on separate rest days to avoid pre-fatiguing muscles. On upper/lower days, add 20 to 30 minutes of low to moderate intensity cardio (incline walking or cycling) after your weights. On PPL, you can add cardio after push or pull days, but avoid hard cardio before leg day or after heavy deadlifts. For fat loss, schedule 3 to 4 cardio sessions per week on non-lifting days or after upper body sessions. High intensity cardio should be separated from lifting by at least 6 hours or done on rest days.

instruction: What is a good full-body workout for someone who can only train 2 days per week?
output: Day 1: goblet squats 3x8-12, bench press 3x8-12, bent-over rows 3x8-12, overhead press 3x10-15, leg curls 3x12-15, planks 3x30-60 seconds. Day 2: Romanian deadlifts 3x8-12, pull-ups or lat pulldowns 3x6-10, leg press 3x10-15, incline dumbbell press 3x8-12, face pulls 3x15-20, hanging leg raises 3x10-15. Since you only train twice weekly, each session should include 6 to 8 exercises and you can train closer to failure (0 to 2 reps in reserve). Add 1 to 2 sets per exercise compared to a 3-day split to compensate for lower frequency. Progress by adding weight or reps each week.

instruction: How do I balance strength and hypertrophy on an upper/lower split?
output: Use a heavy/light split: upper A (heavy strength): bench press 3x5, rows 3x5, overhead press 3x5, then add 2x8-12 accessory lifts. Upper B (light hypertrophy): incline press 3x8-12, lat pulldown 3x8-12, lateral raises 3x12-15, then 3x10-15 arm work. Lower A (heavy): squats 3x5, Romanian deadlifts 3x8, then leg press 3x10-12. Lower B (light): deadlifts 3x5, front squats 3x8-10, leg curls 3x12-15. This approach builds strength on compounds and volume on accessories, giving you the best of both worlds. Heavy days use 80 to 90 percent of your 1RM, light days use 65 to 75 percent.

instruction: Is PPL or upper/lower better for bringing up a weak chest?
output: Upper/lower allows you to add extra chest volume more easily because you have two upper days per week, each with 2 to 3 chest exercises. On PPL, chest is only trained on push days (2 days per week) but you can add an extra chest exercise on both push days. For a weak chest, either split works if you increase frequency to 2 to 3 chest sessions weekly and prioritize chest first in your workout. Example on upper/lower: upper A do 4 chest exercises, upper B do 3 chest exercises, total 14 to 18 sets weekly. On PPL, add a third push day or do chest on leg day as a finisher. The split matters less than total weekly volume and exercise selection.

instruction: How long should each workout be on full-body, upper/lower, and PPL?
output: Full-body: 45 to 60 minutes for 5 to 7 exercises with 90 seconds rest on compounds. Upper/lower: 50 to 70 minutes for 6 to 9 exercises, with upper days often slightly longer due to more muscle groups. PPL: 60 to 90 minutes for 7 to 10 exercises per session; push and pull days are usually longer than leg days. If you are short on time, reduce rest periods (60 seconds for compounds, 30 to 45 for isolations) or superset opposing muscle groups (e.g., bench press with rows). Do not cut warm-ups or compound lift volume; cut isolation exercises instead.

instruction: Can I run an upper/lower split as a beginner?
output: Yes, beginners can run upper/lower, but a 3-day full-body is often better for learning movement patterns with higher frequency. If you prefer upper/lower, start with 3 days per week (e.g., upper, lower, upper) then progress to 4 days after 4 to 8 weeks. Keep volume lower: 5 to 6 exercises per session, 2 to 3 sets each, focusing on form over weight. Avoid advanced techniques like drop sets or failure training. After 3 months on upper/lower, you can add more exercises and increase intensity. Many beginner programs like StrongLifts or Starting Strength are full-body for a reason: more practice per week on key lifts.

instruction: What is the difference between a bro split and upper/lower or PPL?
output: A bro split trains one muscle group per day: chest Monday, back Tuesday, shoulders Wednesday, legs Thursday, arms Friday. This hits each muscle once weekly, which research shows is less effective for growth than twice weekly frequency. Upper/lower and PPL train each muscle 2 times per week, providing more total weekly volume and better muscle protein synthesis stimulation. Bro splits work for advanced bodybuilders using high volume (20+ sets per muscle) or steroids, but natural lifters see 20 to 50 percent more growth on twice weekly splits. Unless you are very advanced or love the routine, choose upper/lower or PPL instead.

instruction: How do I schedule rest days on a 5-day upper/lower or PPL?
output: For 5-day upper/lower: upper Monday, lower Tuesday, upper Wednesday, lower Thursday, upper Friday, rest Saturday and Sunday. This gives upper body 3x weekly and lower 2x weekly, which works if you want to prioritize upper body. For 5-day PPL: push Monday, pull Tuesday, legs Wednesday, push Thursday, pull Friday, rest Saturday and Sunday. This hits push and pull 2x weekly, legs 1x weekly; add leg work on pull day if needed. Another option: PPL rest upper lower (6 days) then take an extra rest day. Listen to your recovery; if you feel run down after 3 weeks, switch to 4 days or add a mid-week rest.
